purpose: The ways a running C# program can HOLD layer-1 content. Not layer 1 (the data is fixed), not layer 3 (no operations beyond load-and-read-back), not the type system.
reference: language knowledge, checked against ../type_vocabulary/raw/csharp.types.json as a candidate checklist only (superseded node; not a decision instrument). No c# toolchain was reachable in the sandbox; this file is enumerated but not executed here.

nothing.note: an absent reference; the hole names a declared reference kind.
a struct wrapping a value plus a present flag; the hole is a flipped flag, not a missing address.
the widest reference kind; every reference kind's absence collapses to this same null.

truth.note: two values, one byte, no numeric side (unlike C, bool does not implicitly convert to int).

whole.note: signed 32-bit; the default integer literal type, so it refuses everything past its own width.
signed 64-bit; the usual whole-number holder, refuses past i64 max.
unsigned 64-bit; reaches u64 max exactly, has no room below zero.
unbounded whole number; every edge in the data file fits with room to spare.
signed 16-bit; the narrow end, refuses everything above roughly 32000.

fractional.note: IEEE double; the default fractional literal type.
IEEE single; holds every base value at lower precision, needs the f suffix or the literal defaults to double.
exact base-10 fixed point; no bit pattern for NaN or infinity, so those spellings must go through a checked cast that throws.

text.note: immutable run of utf-16 code units; the default text holder.
an array of utf-16 code units; a codepoint past the basic plane spans two elements.
mutable text buffer, appended and read back as a string.
holds text only as encoded bytes; the codepoints are gone until decoded.

sequence.note: fixed length once allocated, one declared element kind.
growable ordered run, one declared element kind.
a read-only window over a growable run that lives elsewhere.

probes.mixed: ReadOnlyCollection<long> v = new ReadOnlyCollection<long>(new List<long>{1, "two", 3.0, true, 0});

sequence.note: ordered run open at both ends, one declared element kind.

probes.mixed: LinkedList<long> v = new LinkedList<long>(new long[]{1, "two", 3.0, true, 0});

sequence.note: fixed length, and each position may be a different kind; the c# sequence holder that takes the mixed row. A single element needs ValueTuple.Create since (x,) is not tuple syntax here.
boxes every element; the one array kind that takes the mixed row, at the cost of losing the declared element kind entirely.

probes.mixed: object[] v = new object[]{1L, "two", 3.0, true, null};

keyed.note: name to element, no order guaranteed.
keyed.read: ((System.Func<string>)(() => { var ks = new List<string>(v.Keys); ks.Sort(); return string.Join(",", ks) + "|" + v.Count; }))()

keyed.note: names fixed when the shape is declared, and C# forbids declaring a type inside a method body, so every probe of this entry shares one set of top-level record declarations; the odd keys cannot be spelled as record parameter names at all, not even locally, so those probes fall back to an anonymous-type attempt that the parser refuses outright.

probes.nested: var v = new RN(new Dictionary<string, List<long>>{{"inner", new List<long>{1, 2}}});

keyed.spelling: struct S { public long a; } new S{a=1};
keyed.note: a value-type field bag; same top-level-only restriction and same identifier refusal as the record entry.

keyed.note: a reference-type field bag; ToString() is not overridden here, so the read-back only ever surfaces the type name, not the fields — the finding for this cell.

nesting.note: nesting by repeating the same holder; every level must carry the same declared kind.

nesting.note: boxes every element; nesting is just an object[] holding more object[] or Dictionary<string,object>.

probes.seq_in_map: object[] v = new object[]{new Dictionary<string, object>{{"outer", new Dictionary<string, object>{{"inner", new object[]{1L, 2L}}}}}};

identity.spelling: struct Triple{...}; var v = new List<Triple>{s,s};
identity.note: a value type has no reference identity at all; a list of structs stores independent copies, so mutating one never reaches the other, and even two boxed copies of the same source struct compare as different objects.

identity.spelling: class Box{...}; var v = new List<Box>{s,s};
identity.note: reference types default to shared storage; two positions can name one object, and a self field can hold a reference to its own object.

identity.pre:
using System.Collections.Generic;
class Box { public List<long> items; public Box(List<long> i) { items = i; } }
identity.note: arrays of a reference kind hold addresses, not copies; an object[] can even hold a reference to the very array it sits in.
